title: Take a wheelchair's locked armrest off, lifting it square out of both sockets, and lay it down
instruction: Take the armrest off the wheelchair and lay it down on the table on your side of the chair, so the patient can slide across to the bed.
context: Nursing assistants (O*NET 31-1131.00, about 1.3 million in the US) and home health and personal care aides (31-1122.00, about 3.7 million) take off the armrest on the bed side of a wheelchair before every sliding-board or lateral transfer. The armrest is locked in its sockets: its release tab has to be held back while it is lifted, and its two posts, 20 cm apart and 10 cm deep, drawn straight up together, as lifted by one end they bind. The 1.2 kg armrest is then laid down on its side, not dropped.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Wheelchair left side frame, black powder-coated steel, fixed to the table with its outer side toward the arms and its front toward -y: two arm sockets, square steel tubes 2.5 cm inside with 0.3 cm walls on 1 cm floor plates, mouths 11 cm above the table, centred at x 46, y -10 (front) and y 10 (rear); the front socket's front wall (toward -y) has a window 1.6 cm wide, 4.6 to 6.7 cm above the table. On the seat side of each socket a 2.5 x 2.5 cm frame upright, 13.5 cm tall; a 2.5 x 2.5 cm seat rail at 11 to 13.5 cm height from y -25 to 22.5; a back cane at y 20 to 22.5 rising to 42 cm; a blue seat (x 50.05 to 86, y -24 to 20, 11 to 15 cm high) and blue back (y 20 to 21.5, 15 to 42 cm high). Removable desk-length armrest, 1.2 kg: a black vinyl pad 26 x 5.5 x 3.8 cm on two square steel posts 2.2 x 2.2 cm, centres 20 cm apart, 29.2 cm long below the pad; it stands with its posts on the socket floors, 10 cm deep in the sockets, pad top 34 cm above the table. Lock: one 50 g part that slides 0.7 cm along the armrest toward its rear (+y) against a 0.4 N per mm spring: a red tab (3.5 x 2.4 x 1.2 cm) standing out of the front post toward the arms, 21 to 22.2 cm above the table, and a steel catch (1.2 x 1.0 x 1.5 cm) standing 0.5 cm out of the front post's front face into the socket's window, 5 to 6.5 cm above the table.
scoring: Measured with a ruler, a protractor and a photo; the armrest's centre is the point on its centreline 16.5 cm up the posts from their feet. 0 if the armrest was ever let fall (moving down faster than 0.8 m/s with its lowest point more than 5 cm above the table). Otherwise: 1.0 if both posts are out of their sockets, its centre is at least 10 cm out from the sockets' line toward the arms, and it lies on the table on its side (tipped at least 75 degrees from upright, its lowest point within 3 mm of the table), at rest (moving slower than 1 cm/s and turning slower than 0.05 rad/s, about 3 degrees/s) for 1 s; else the furthest it got: 0.75 if both posts were out with its centre at least 10 cm out from the sockets' line; 0.5 if both posts were out of their sockets (each foot 5 mm above its socket's mouth, or 3 cm to the side of the socket's axis); 0.25 if it was lifted 2 cm (which needs the lock released); else 0.
reset_notes: Hold the red tab back, stand the armrest's two posts back in their sockets until they rest on the socket floors, and let go of the tab so the catch springs out into the window.
fidelity: Rigid boxes at full size and weight. Posts are 2.2 cm square (real: round tubes) in sockets with 1.5 mm clearance a side. The lock is a sprung slider: a tab, sized for gripper fingers, slides a square catch out of a socket window (real: spring lever or plunger in a hole). Only the chair's left side frame is modelled, fixed as a braked chair with the socket floors at table height (real: ~45 cm up); wheels, footrests and right side are omitted. Light angular damping.
